name: Embodied AI
summary: General-purpose robotics reaching the point where one model drives many physical tasks without per-task engineering.
substrate_test: Passes in principle. A single policy that generalises across tasks is a substrate; a robot programmed per task is a machine tool. Which of the two is actually being built is the open question, and demonstrations are chosen to obscure it.
threshold_unlock: Unresolved. No consumer or small-business interaction exists, so the revelation test — a non-specialist uses it and returns to it unprompted a week later — has not yet been available to run.
distribution_test: Fails by construction. Every unit is physical, so marginal cost stays high and distribution is logistics rather than download. This is the strongest argument that it scales like an industrial theme and not like the internet.
bottleneck_test: Passes. Harmonic drives, rare-earth magnets, high-torque actuators and cell energy density. Overlaps critical-minerals-security, which means part of this candidate is already investable through an active theme.
graduation_criteria: A published cost per robot-hour below the local loaded labour cost for one named task, sustained across four quarters, disclosed by a company that reports unit economics rather than demonstration footage.

name: Orbital Economics
summary: What becomes economic at $100-200/kg to orbit that is not economic at $1,500/kg.
substrate_test: Passes. Cheap mass to orbit is an input to many industries rather than a product in itself.
threshold_unlock: The central unknown, and this row exists to record that. No application has yet been named that is uneconomic at Falcon 9 pricing and economic at Starship pricing. An honest empty answer here is more useful than a speculative one, because it dates the moment the answer arrives.
distribution_test: Fails. Physical goods, licensed spectrum and national launch approvals.
bottleneck_test: Passes. Launch cadence, orbital slots, spectrum rights and deep-space network capacity are all rivalrous and administratively rationed.
graduation_criteria: Full reuse demonstrated with published per-kg pricing, AND one named application booking commercial revenue that is arithmetically impossible at Falcon 9 pricing. Both, not either.

name: Programmable Biology
summary: Biological manufacture becoming a design problem rather than a discovery problem.
substrate_test: Passes. Programmable biology is a substrate in the same sense that a programmable computer is one.
threshold_unlock: Partially met, and repeatedly false-started. Reading biology crossed its threshold years ago and the sequencing cost curve is the most dramatic in the whole file. Writing biology has not. The theme has produced a revelation for specialists and for nobody else, which is the pattern that preceded three prior disappointments in this field.
distribution_test: Mixed. Designs are digital and free to copy; the manufactured output is physical, regulated, and slow to approve.
bottleneck_test: Unclear, which is a weakness. Fermentation capacity and enzyme supply are candidates, but neither is demonstrably scarce, and a theme with no bottleneck offers no obvious way to hold it.
graduation_criteria: Cost per synthesised base below $0.001 at commercial scale, AND volume growth in at least two non-pharmaceutical end markets that is independent of grant funding.

name: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
summary: Error-corrected quantum hardware crossing from physics demonstration to commercial computation.
substrate_test: Fails as currently understood, and this is the row's most important field. Known quantum advantage is confined to a narrow class of problems. A tool for factoring and simulation is not a general-purpose substrate however it is marketed, and the distinction is exactly what separated the internet from 3D printing.
threshold_unlock: Not met. No commercially valuable problem has been solved on quantum hardware faster or cheaper than the best classical method.
distribution_test: Passes, if access is sold as a cloud API rather than as hardware.
bottleneck_test: Passes. Dilution refrigerators, helium-3, cryogenic control electronics and specialised photonics are genuinely scarce and already have listed suppliers.
graduation_criteria: One commercially valuable problem — not a sampling benchmark chosen because quantum hardware happens to win it — solved at lower total cost than the best classical method, and reproduced independently.

name: Long-Duration Energy Storage
summary: Storage economics extending from hours to days, which changes what a grid can be built from.
substrate_test: Fails, and correctly so. Storage is an input to an existing theme rather than a substrate of its own. Recorded here so that it is not mistaken for a next wave when it is an extension of a current one.
threshold_unlock: Arguably crossed already at four-hour duration, and unresolved at one hundred hours. The two durations are different businesses with different chemistries and should not be tracked as one thing.
bottleneck_test: Passes, and is already held through age-of-electricity.
graduation_criteria: Not applicable. This candidate is tracked as evidence feeding an existing theme rather than as a graduation prospect.

name: Neural Interfaces
summary: Bandwidth between nervous systems and computers rising fast enough to support uses beyond clinical restoration.
substrate_test: Unresolved. Restoration of lost function and augmentation of intact function are different markets with different regulatory paths, and only the first currently exists.
threshold_unlock: Not met and possibly distant. The threshold requires an invasive procedure, which is a behaviour change far larger than the one consumer VR failed to obtain.
distribution_test: Fails. Surgical, regulated and individually fitted.
bottleneck_test: Weak. Electrode materials and implantable ASICs are specialised but not obviously constrained.
graduation_criteria: Channel counts rising at their current rate for a further four years, AND one approved non-restorative indication. The second condition is the one that has never been met.
